1. All possible water samples in the MN River.
2. One water sample from MN River.
3. 40 water samples
4. Localized Nitrogen quantities could bias the results. Taking samples from randomly determined locations would be better representative of Nitrogen in the river.
5. Yes. The sample size is large and the distribution is not largely skewed.
6. $H_0$: The long run average quantity of Nitrogen in the MN River is equal to 4.19 mg/L. $H_A$: The long run average quantity of Nitrogen in the MN River is greater than 4.19 mg/L.
7. $H_0:\mu=4.19 \text{ vs. }H_A:\mu>4.19$
8. $$\frac{4.23-4.19}{0.19/\sqrt{40}}=1.331485$$. This value is inside the 2's and rejects the null hypothesis.
9. $$4.23\pm2\cdot 0.19/\sqrt{40}=(4.169917,4.290083)$$. The value of 4.19 is inside this interval and thus a plausible value for the average quantity of Nitrogen. This rejects the null hypothesis.
10. There is not evidence to conclude that the true average quantity of Nitrogen in mg/L is greater than the historical average of 4.19 mg/L. 
11. The long-run proportion of water samples with sulfate quantities that exceed the safe limit, $\pi$
12. $$\frac{11}{40}\pm 2\cdot \sqrt{\frac{(11/40)(1-11/40)}{40}}=(0.1337998,0.4162002)$$. We are 95% confident that the true proportion of water samples from the MN River that have sulfate quantities that exceed the safe limit is between 0.1337998 and 0.4162002. 
13. Since we can expect the proportion of samples with unsafe sulfate levels to change with different samples, we can test $H_0:\pi=0.1\text{ vs. }H_A:\pi>0.1$. Since 0.1 is less than the entire confidence interval, we can conclude with 95% confidence that the true proportion of water samples from the MN River would be greater than 0.1.
